title: Venezuela Firms Vow Output Doubling as US Strikes Iran's Export Tankers; US Gasoline Hits Record $4.03
subhead: The US-Iran maritime conflict escalated sharply Saturday as US forces destroyed three Iranian crude carriers near Kharg Island after IRGC ballistic missiles were fired at Navy ships, while in Caracas Chevron, Eni and GE Vernova committed to expansions Washington says will more than double Venezuelan output. Record pump prices and depressed Hormuz transit frame both stories.

sections.heading: US Sinks Three Iranian Export Tankers After Missiles Fired at Navy Ships
sections.body:
The most significant escalation in the Gulf war since the Hormuz lull broke: US military forces struck and destroyed three Iranian crude oil carriers near Kharg Island and in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy warships, according to CENTCOM reporting carried by CNN, the New York Post and other outlets. Kharg Island is the critical export hub for Iranian oil shipments, and the tankers targeted are described as part of Iran's 'shadow network' of crude carriers — the same fleet that has kept roughly 1 million bpd of Iranian exports moving with transponders deactivated despite sanctions and blockade, as prior tracking data showed.

Iran responded with a warning that continued US maritime restrictions and attacks on its shipping could trigger 'harsher and wider' strikes (Palestine Chronicle), and the IRGC separately said it had fired several ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and destroyer it accused of harassing Iranian ships (Republic World). The tit-for-tat around Iranian export infrastructure marks a qualitative shift from the earlier phase, in which strikes hit military targets and proxies — now the US is directly destroying the vessels that move Iran's oil revenue.
sections.whyItMatters: By targeting the tankers rather than just the shore, Washington is now striking at Iran's export revenue directly. The question is whether this degrades the dark fleet enough to actually cut Iranian exports, or simply pushes more of the trade into smaller, harder-to-track vessels — and whether Tehran's 'harsher' warning turns into attacks on the Gulf oil infrastructure it has so far spared.

sections.heading: Chevron, Eni and GE Vernova Commit to Venezuela Expansions as Output Set to Double
sections.body:
Several international energy firms — Chevron, Eni, and GE Vernova among them — signed commitments on Wednesday in Caracas to expand oil projects, in a ceremony overseen by interim President Delcy Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright (Reuters). Wright said the deals will lead to more than a doubling of Venezuelan crude production in the next few years, and separately reiterated that Beijing will have no debt claims on revenue from new Venezuelan output despite Caracas owing China roughly $10 billion.

President Trump called the accord the 'greatest ever' oil deal, but US oil executives are raising concerns that the arrangement — built around the North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) venture holding 100-year rights to 17 oilfields with an estimated 65 billion barrels of reserves, into which Washington took a 35% position via penny warrants — could sideline American firms from real participation (Business Standard, Reuters). Venezuela's interim leadership is betting the investment flood arrives faster than the promised elections, with analysts noting the US may prioritize production over democratic timelines (MSN/Egypt Independent).
sections.whyItMatters: This is the concrete follow-through on a deal previously covered at the framework stage — now named companies with real balance sheets are committed. Whether output genuinely doubles depends on the warrant-and-offtake structure attracting capital without US firms being structurally excluded, and on whether Caracas's $10 billion debt to China can truly be written out of the new production streams.

sections.heading: Record $4.03 Gasoline and Brent Above $95 Keep War Costs at the Pump
sections.body:
US gasoline prices are projected to hit a record $4.03 per gallon for the Labor Day weekend, as the Iran conflict keeps crude elevated (CryptoBriefing), on top of already-record diesel prices. Brent crude finished the week above $95 a barrel, up roughly 6-7%, after volatile trading driven by Hormuz fears against demand worries (Peninsula Qatar, HDFC Sky). Toronto pump prices hit 183.9 Canadian cents a litre after another overnight increase on Sept 5 (MSN).

The refined-product squeeze — diesel cracks trading above outright crude — remains the core driver, meaning the war's cost is registering in freight, agriculture and construction rather than only at the crude barrel. Analysts' consensus still holds oil above $80 a barrel through 2026, with weak Chinese demand capping the ceiling even as physical Gulf flows stay disrupted (Reuters poll).
sections.whyItMatters: The record retail figures, landing on a US holiday weekend, translate the abstract barrel price into a directly felt political and economic cost. With diesel already at historic highs, any further tanker-loss disruption to product flows — which is exactly what Saturday's strikes threaten — would keep the squeeze tightening rather than easing.

sections.heading: Hormuz Transit Stays Depressed as LNG Reroutes via Ship-to-Ship
sections.body:
Gulf shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained well below its 10-day average, with only about four commodity vessels transiting on Thursday versus a norm near 15, per Kpler data reported by Reuters. The persistence of the disruption is now forcing structural workarounds: three LNG cargoes loaded in Qatar and the UAE have been transferred between ships outside Hormuz in recent weeks for delivery to India and Japan, according to ship-tracking firms (Reuters, Sept 2). Analysis of the reroute suggests Middle Eastern exporters are rapidly developing alternative routes as Hormuz oil flows plunge from nearly 20 million bpd to an estimated 6-8 million bpd (MSN/Iran war rewrite).

The ship-to-ship transfers are a stopgap — moving cargo at sea between Gulf-loaded vessels and onward carriers that avoid the contested waterway — a logistical patch that keeps contracts alive but adds cost, time and risk of disputes over which vessel is legitimate.
sections.whyItMatters: The LNG ship-to-ship workaround signals that the world's largest gas exporters have concluded Hormuz re-routing is not a temporary spike but a persistent condition requiring procedural adaptation. That normalizes what was once considered an emergency measure — and hints Asian buyers are willing to absorb the added cost to keep supply chains intact.

sections.heading: Bangladesh's Gas Crisis Deepens as India Weighs a Fresh Opening
sections.body:
Gas shortages are crippling Bangladesh's power sector, hitting industry and exports, according to StratNewsGlobal, in a story largely absent from Western coverage. The crisis gives India a fresh opening to expand energy leverage over its neighbor, the analysis notes, as Dhaka struggles to keep plants running amid a broader global LNG price squeeze driven by the Gulf conflict.

Bangladesh — which relies heavily on imported LNG spot cargoes — is exposed on multiple fronts: elevated global gas prices from the Iran war, competition with India and China for spot cargoes, and tight domestic currency reserves that limit how much expensive LNG it can buy. A Business Standard analysis frames the broader pattern of the country becoming an 'energy-importing nation' despite early warnings about the risks of import dependence.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a reminder of how the Gulf war's costs cascade far beyond oil markets into South Asia's poorer gas importers. Bangladesh's distress is India's opportunity — a regional asymmetry that shapes electricity politics across a market of 170 million people and could redraw Dhaka's energy relationships with Delhi.

sections.heading: North Macedonia and Serbia Join the Vertical Gas Corridor
sections.body:
On the pipeline front, North Macedonia and Serbia officially joined the Vertical Gas Corridor, expanding the network's reach, with Baku confirming the two countries will gain access to the Southern Gas Corridor and Azerbaijani gas (AzerNews, Trend, Sept 5). A new North Macedonia-Greece gas link will open access to both LNG and Azerbaijani supply, deepening the Caspian corridor's pull into the Balkans as Europe continues to diversify away from Russian pipeline gas.

The additions tie two more non-EU Balkan states into a supply architecture built around Azerbaijan as anchor producer — a quiet but steady expansion of the Southern Gas Corridor's customer base at a time when Russian volumes to Europe remain constrained by the Ukraine war and sanctions.
sections.whyItMatters: Each new member of the Vertical Corridor hardens an alternative to Russian gas that bypasses Moscow entirely. The corridor's quiet expansion into the Western Balkans, at the geographic margin of EU energy policy, shows diversification is being pursued as much through regional infrastructure as through headline LNG deals.

bottomLine: Saturday's strikes on three Iranian export tankers mark a real step-change in the Gulf war — Washington has moved from hitting military and proxy targets to destroying the very vessels that carry Iran's oil revenue, in direct response to IRGC ballistic missiles fired at Navy warships. The near-term market impact is clear in record US pump prices ($4.03 gasoline, diesel already at historic highs) and Brent holding above $95 with Hormuz transit at a fraction of normal. In parallel, the Venezuela deal moved from framework to contractual commitments as Chevron, Eni and GE Vernova signed on to expansions that Washington says will more than double output — a counterweight project aimed at replacing disrupted Gulf barrels. The strategic through-line: every major player is now adapting to a world in which Hormuz is not reliably open — tankers are being sunk, LNG is being transshipped at sea, alternative routes are being built, and Venezuela's output is being rushed forward as partial compensation.
sources: Reuters (Venezuela deals; Hormuz transit data; LNG ship-to-ship; output doubling; oil price poll), CNN, New York Times, New York Post, Republic World, Palestine Chronicle, CryptoBriefing, Peninsula Qatar, HDFC Sky, Business Standard, MSN/Iran war trade routes, AzerNews, Trend, StratNewsGlobal, Egypt Independent
